titulo.en: It was Saturday and it was sunny

objetivo.en: Tell a complete experience: the setting in the imperfect and what happened in the preterite.

nota.en: Natural thermal pools, a classic stop in Baños.
The tiny drops of water on grass and leaves in the early morning.
No accent here: it is a connector, unlike the question word ¿cuándo?.

explicacion.en: English speakers often use the preterite for every “was” in the past. To describe the setting (the day, the weather), Spanish uses the imperfect: era, hacía.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: Hacía sol y llegábamos a Baños a las cuatro.
erroresFrecuentes.correcto: Hacía sol y llegamos a Baños a las cuatro.

explicacion.en: Arriving at a specific time is a finished event, so it takes the preterite: llegamos. The imperfect is for the background, not for the event that moves the story forward.

texto.en: To tell a story in the past, Spanish uses two tenses together. The imperfect paints the background: what the day was like, the weather, how people or things were. The preterite moves the story forward: the actions that happened, one after another. Era sábado, hacía sol and Daniela estaba cansada describe the setting (it was Saturday, it was sunny, Daniela was tired). Llegamos, fuimos and compré are events (we arrived, we went, I bought). English makes a similar split (“it was sunny” against “we arrived”), but Spanish makes you choose in every sentence. You can join them with cuando: Hacía sol cuando llegamos a Baños. The imperfect gives the background and the preterite gives the event. Remember the forms: era (from ser) is irregular, hacía comes from hacer, and estaba comes from estar. Weather in a story is usually in the imperfect: hacía sol, hacía frío.
Left: how things were (imperfect). Right: what happened (preterite). Tap each phrase to hear it.

titulo.en: What if we go to Otavalo?

objetivo.en: Suggest and plan a trip to Otavalo: when you leave, how you travel and what the weather will be.

nota.en: Followed by the present tense: ¿Y si vamos?
Also followed by the present tense.

traduccion.en: the return trip / the way back

nota.en: For a woman: la artesana.
Otavalo is famous for its market of handicrafts.

explicacion.en: After ¿y si…? (what if…?), Spanish uses the present tense: ¿Y si vamos…? Do not use the future there, even though the trip is in the future.

erroresFrecuentes.correcto: Vamos a salir a las siete.

explicacion.en: The plan with ir needs the little word a before the infinitive: vamos a salir. English has no word between “going” and “to leave”, so it is easy to forget.
Salir has an irregular future stem: sald-. Add the endings to that stem: saldré, saldremos, saldrán.
To suggest something, the phrase is ¿qué tal si…? (how about…?). Without si, ¿qué tal? just asks how things are going.

texto.en: This class is a review: you already know every tool in it, and now you combine them to plan an outing. You need three moves. First, suggest: ¿Y si vamos a Otavalo? or ¿Qué tal si salimos temprano? Both take the present tense after si, and you can answer or counter-suggest with Mejor el sábado. Second, plan: vamos a salir a las siete uses ir + a + infinitive and sounds natural and close. Third, talk about what will happen with the future tense: tomaremos el bus, llegaremos a las nueve, saldremos a las siete. The regular future is the infinitive plus an ending, as in tomar → tomaremos, and a few verbs change their stem: salir → saldremos, hacer → haremos. For the weather, hará is the future of hace: Por la mañana hará frío. Between friends, tú is the natural way to talk.

nota.en: Suggest: ¿y si + present?
Suggest: ¿qué tal si + present?

titulo.en: Could you change the size for me?

objetivo.en: Handle a purchase at the Otavalo market: ask the price, politely ask for another size and pay.

nota.en: Ch sounds like the ch in “church”: “POHN-choh”.
At many markets you can ask for a better price.
The frame where fabric is woven by hand.

traduccion.en: to change for me / to exchange for me

nota.en: Cambiar + me: ¿Podría cambiarme la talla? = Could you change the size for me?

explicacion.en: The garment is the subject: it fits me big, so the verb agrees with it: queda. Me quedo would mean “I stay”.
Pequeño agrees with the garment. El poncho is masculine, so pequeño; la bufanda is feminine, so pequeña. Grande does not change: me queda grande for both.
With a vendor you use usted, so the verb is podría. Podrías is the tú form, for friends.
When it means la talla, the pronoun is feminine: se la cambio. It matches the thing, not the person.

texto.en: This class is a review: you combine forms you already know to shop at a market. You do four things. Ask the price: ¿Cuánto cuesta el poncho? and the seller answers Son quince dólares. Say how it fits: me queda grande (it is too big on me) or me queda pequeño (too small). Queda is singular because the garment is one item (quedan for several), and pequeño or pequeña agrees with it too: el poncho → pequeño, la bufanda → pequeña. Ask politely with usted: Me gustaría el poncho azul. ¿Podría cambiarme la talla? Podría and me gustaría are the conditional, the polite form. Finally, compare and pay: Esta bufanda es más barata que el poncho. The seller says Su vuelto, cinco dólares. When the seller answers Se la cambio, se replaces le (to you) because le + la becomes se la: I will change it (the size) for you. With a vendor you use usted.
The conditional is the polite way to ask or to say what you would like. Tap each form to hear it.
Both speak with usted. Tap each phrase to hear it.

explicacion.en: The weather that sets the scene takes the imperfect: hacía. The preterite is for the event that follows, llegamos.

explicacion.en: To say two things are equal, use tan… como (as… as). Más… que is for “more… than”, so don't mix que into the equal comparison.

texto.en: You have reached the end of the level, so this class puts four tools together. To tell about the past, use the imperfect for the setting, as in era sábado, hacía sol, and the preterite for the events, as in llegamos, fuimos, compré. To talk about plans, use the future: viajaremos, compraremos, llegaremos, and the irregular haré, saldremos. To compare, use más… que for “more… than” and tan… como for “as… as”. To ask politely, use the conditional: ¿Podría…? and me gustaría… Remember that for -ar and -ir verbs the nosotros form of the preterite looks like the present: llegamos, salimos. The sentence around it tells you which one it is: ayer llegamos is past. Look at the tables, then use them to tell about your trip to Baños and announce the trip to Otavalo.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: Era domingo y llovió cuando salimos.
erroresFrecuentes.correcto: Era domingo y llovía cuando salimos.

explicacion.en: The weather that sets the scene takes the imperfect: llovía. The event that follows takes the preterite: salimos.
After he, has, ha… use the participle, as in estado, visitado, comido, not the infinitive. English also uses a participle here: “have been”, not “have be”.

texto.en: This is the final test of the level. It checks four things you already know. First, telling a story in the past: the imperfect gives the setting, as in era sábado, hacía frío, llovía, and the preterite gives the events, as in llegamos, salimos, fuimos. Second, talking about experiences with the present perfect: ¿Has estado alguna vez en Cuenca? Sí, he estado una vez. Nunca he estado en Mindo. Third, giving advice: deberías + infinitive, as in Deberías avisar a la secretaria. Fourth, asking whether something is allowed: ¿Se puede usar el salón? Sí, se puede, or No, está prohibido. Take it calmly: you already know all of this. The tables show the forms you need, so read them before you start.
He, has, ha, hemos and han are always followed by the participle: estado.
Deberías + infinitive: you should… Use it with a friend (tú).
